title: One idea per shot
text: A shot carries a single thing to understand, and everything in it serves that thing. When a frame asks the eye to read a headline, a chart and a caption at once, the viewer reads none of them. Cut the idea in two and give each half its own shot, even if each is short. Many short, clear shots hold attention better than a few crowded ones.
see: Say what the shot shows in one sentence. If the sentence needs an 'and', there are two shots.

title: The subject shown up close
text: Show the thing the film is about large, framed tight, with its real detail legible: the interface at full fidelity, the product filling the frame, the number big enough to read from across a room. A small subject floating in empty space reads as a diagram of a film rather than a film. Crop into the part that matters and let the rest leave the frame.
see: Pause on a frame. The subject should still be recognisable and readable on a phone held at arm's length.

title: A frame with a light
text: Treat light as a material: a soft glow behind the subject, a rim along an edge, a gradient that suggests where the light comes from. Light gives flat shapes volume and tells the eye where to land. It can be quiet, a hint of falloff in the corner, or loud, a beam across the frame, but the frame should never be a uniform plate with things pasted on it.
see: Cover the content with a hand: is anything left that suggests a place, a surface or a source of light?

title: One accent held for the whole film
text: Choose neutrals for most of the surface and one accent colour for what matters, then hold it from the first frame to the last. Because the accent is rare, it carries meaning wherever it appears: a price, a button, a key word. A second accent is allowed only when it plays a different role, such as warning against confirmation. A rainbow of equal colours says nothing.
see: List the colours that appear over the whole film. More than one saturated colour in the same role is a drift.

title: Few sizes, short lines
text: Set the type in two or three sizes only, with a clear jump between them, and keep each line to a handful of words. A large size for the idea, a smaller one for its support, and nothing in between competing. Short lines can be read in the time the shot is on screen; paragraphs cannot. If a sentence will not fit in a few words, the shot is carrying too much.
see: Count the distinct sizes across the film. The ratio between neighbours should be obvious at a glance.

title: Type enters on the cut
text: Let words arrive with the picture, on the same beat as the cut or the move, rather than drifting in a moment late. When the type and the cut agree, the shot feels designed; when type lags behind, the viewer sees the machinery. A short stagger between lines is fine as long as the first line lands with the cut.
see: Scrub through the cut frame by frame. The first line should be in place within a few frames of the new picture.

title: An element of one shot becomes the next
text: Carry something across the cut: a button that grows into a sphere, a line that becomes the path of the next move, a colour that floods into the next background. A match on shape, position or movement tells the viewer that the two shots belong together and lets the cut disappear. It costs one deliberate choice and replaces any need for a stock transition.
see: Look at the last frame of one shot beside the first of the next. Something should line up.

title: Real-looking detail in every frame
text: Fill interfaces and objects with believable specifics: real names, plausible figures, avatars, row labels, small status marks. Detail is what makes a frame look like something that exists. Placeholders and round numbers announce that nothing is behind the picture. The detail does not need to be read; it needs to be there, and to be right where the viewer does look.
see: Zoom into the corner of an interface. If it is empty or says placeholder text, the frame is not finished.

title: The hero moment prepared by a silence
text: The moment the film is remembered for lands harder when something is taken away just before it: the music thins, the motion stills, a beat of nothing. Contrast makes the peak. Then give the hero its cue, the loudest hit and the biggest move of the film, and let it ring before moving on. If everything is loud, nothing is the climax.
see: Look at the loudness and the motion in the second before the hero. It should be lower than the hero by a clear margin.

title: The camera moves with intent
text: Every camera move answers a question: push in to reveal the detail that matters, pull back to show scale, pan to follow the eye from one thing to the next. A move with a purpose has a start, an ease and a rest, and it ends on a composition worth holding. A drift without a reason makes the whole frame feel unsteady.
see: For each move, say what the viewer is meant to notice at the end of it. If there is no answer, remove the move.

title: Planes separated by depth
text: Give the frame a foreground, a middle and a background, and separate them: different scale, a touch of blur on what is out of focus, a shadow, a different speed when the camera moves. Layers that move together look pasted; layers that part slightly look like a place. Depth also tells the eye where to look, because the sharp plane is the subject.
see: Nudge the camera in your head: would the layers slide past each other, or stay glued?

title: An ending that says where to go
text: Close with the one thing the viewer should do or remember: the name, the address, the next step. Give it room, a held frame long enough to read twice, and strip everything else away. The ending should feel inevitable, as if the whole film were walking towards it. A film that simply stops leaves the viewer with nothing to do.
see: Freeze the last second. Could someone act on what is on screen?

title: Contrast of scale between two shots
text: Follow a very large frame with a very small one, or a close detail with a wide view. The change of scale across the cut is felt as rhythm even when nothing else changes. A film in which every shot has the same size of subject is monotonous however busy it is; alternating scales gives the eye something to do at each cut.
see: Line up thumbnails of the film's shots. The size of the main subject should vary along the row.

title: Holding a frame long enough to read
text: Words need time: about a third of a second a word, plus a beat to take it in. Hold the frame for that time after the text is fully on screen, not including its entrance. Rushing the reading to fit a fast edit makes the film feel frantic rather than energetic. If the edit cannot hold, reduce the words, not the time.
see: Read the text aloud at a normal pace from the moment it settles. If the cut comes first, it is too fast.

title: A cut on the downbeat, or on the phrase
text: Cuts can land on the strong beat of a bar, which feels driving and precise, or on the end of a musical phrase, which feels breathing and natural. Choose one logic for a passage and keep to it. Cutting on every beat for a long time becomes a drumbeat; cutting off the beat all the time feels careless. Vary the two on purpose.
see: Tap along with the music while watching the cuts. They should agree or disagree consistently, not randomly.

title: Motion that answers the sound
text: A hit in the music or a sound effect should have a movement to match: an element snapping into place, a flash, a shake that settles. When picture and sound agree, each makes the other feel stronger. Match the weight, a heavy sound for a heavy move and a light tick for a small one, and leave moments of silence where nothing moves and nothing sounds.
see: Mute the film, then play it with only the sound. Do the impacts line up with something visible?

title: Negative space as a choice
text: Empty space is part of the composition when it is placed on purpose: around a title to give it weight, on one side of a subject to leave room for motion, between two things to separate them. Space that is simply what was left over feels accidental. Decide where the emptiness goes and make the content push against it.
see: Ask whether the empty area could be moved elsewhere without anyone noticing. If so, it was leftover.

title: A data story's one number
text: Among all the figures a chart could show, pick the one that carries the story and make it the largest thing on screen. Let the rest of the chart recede as context. Count it up, or draw the line to it, so the viewer watches it arrive. A chart that gives every value equal weight asks the viewer to do the analysis themselves.
see: Ask what number the viewer should repeat to a friend. It should be the biggest mark on screen.

title: A talking video covered every ten to twenty seconds
text: When a person speaks to camera for a long stretch, give the eye something new at regular intervals: an illustration of what is being said, a key word set large, a change of framing. The speaker stays the anchor, and the additions come and go. The rhythm of the additions should follow the speech, arriving as an idea starts and leaving as it ends.
see: Look at the longest stretch where only the speaker is on screen. Beyond twenty seconds, the eye will drift.

title: A title over the speaker between illustrations
text: Between two illustrations, a short title or key phrase set over the speaker keeps the screen active without taking the person away. Place it where the frame is quiet, away from the face, and let it enter on the stress of the sentence. One or two words are enough. It names the idea the speaker is about to illustrate.
see: Check that the title never covers the face and leaves the screen before the next illustration enters.

title: A rhythm of shot lengths
text: Shots of the same length make a metronome. Vary them: a run of quick shots building energy, then one longer shot that lets the viewer breathe, then a quick run again. The long shot is felt as long only because of the short ones around it. Plan the lengths as a pattern that rises towards the hero, rather than letting them fall out of the content.
see: Write down the length of each shot. A flat list of similar numbers is a flat rhythm.

title: An opening that earns the next five seconds
text: Start on the thing that makes the film worth watching: the claim, the surprise, the most striking picture. Do not open on a logo, a loading animation or a slow fade from nothing. The first seconds decide whether the rest is seen. Establish the look at the same time, so the opening is a promise of the style as well as of the subject.
see: Watch only the first three seconds. Would you keep watching?

title: A restrained vocabulary of motion
text: Pick a small set of movements, one way to enter, one way to leave, one ease, and use them everywhere. Repetition makes the film feel like one hand made it, and lets the few exceptions mean something. Variety for its own sake, a different transition on every cut, reads as a showreel of effects rather than a film.
see: List how each element enters. If every one enters differently, the vocabulary is not restrained.

title: Eased moves that settle
text: Almost nothing in the world moves at a constant speed. Let moves start gently, accelerate, and slow into their final position so the eye can follow the end of the move and read what has arrived. A move that stops abruptly or glides at one speed looks mechanical. Give the largest elements the slowest, softest eases, and the small ones quick ones.
see: Look at the spacing of positions across a move. Even spacing means constant speed; the ends should be tighter.

title: Staggered entrances
text: When several things enter together, start them a few frames apart, in the order of importance or of reading. The stagger turns a block into a sequence and tells the viewer where to look first. Keep it short enough that the group still reads as one gesture, and slightly uneven so it does not tick like a machine.
see: Count the frames between the starts of grouped elements. Zero is a block; the same gap every time is a tick.

title: Hierarchy by scale before colour
text: Make the most important thing the biggest, then reach for weight, then for colour. Scale is understood instantly and survives a small screen and a glance; colour alone is easily lost. When three things compete, decide which is first, second and third, and let the sizes say so. Equal sizes tell the viewer the order does not matter.
see: Squint at the frame until it blurs. The order in which things stand out is the order the viewer will read.

title: Contrast that serves reading
text: Text must stand clearly off what is behind it, at the size and on the screen where it will be watched. Light on dark and dark on light both work; mid-tone on mid-tone does not. When the background is busy, calm it under the words with a plate, a blur or a shadow rather than making the words louder. Check the worst frame, not the best.
see: Look at the text over its busiest moment of background. If you hesitate, the viewer will not read it.

title: One material language
text: Choose how things are made in this film, flat paper, glass, brushed metal, grain and ink, and keep to it. Surfaces that share a language, with the same kind of edge, shadow and texture, look like parts of one world. Mixing a photograph with flat vector shapes and glossy renders in one frame breaks the world unless the mixture itself is the idea.
see: Name the material of every object in a frame. If the names do not belong together, the frame is mismatched.

title: Texture gives a surface life
text: A touch of grain, paper fibre, noise or a slow gradient shift removes the sterile look of a perfectly flat fill. Texture should be subtle enough not to compete with the content and consistent enough to feel like a property of the world. It also hides banding in smooth gradients and gives compression something natural to work on.
see: Look at an empty area of the frame at full size. Perfectly uniform means nothing is there.

title: A palette that comes from the subject
text: Draw the colours from the thing the film is about: its product, its place, its season, its brand. A palette that belongs to the subject feels discovered, not applied. Pick a dominant tone, a supporting neutral and one accent, and test them together on the hardest frame. Borrowing a fashionable palette that has nothing to do with the subject makes every film look alike.
see: Cover the title. Do the colours still suggest what the film is about?

title: Choose the plate, dark or light, for the mood
text: A dark ground makes light and colour glow and suits precision, night, technology and drama; a light ground feels open, calm, printed and trustworthy. Neither is neutral. Decide once, then build the whole film on it, including the interfaces drawn inside it. Switching plates between scenes is possible as a deliberate contrast, but never by accident.
see: Ask why the ground is the tone it is. A reason about the subject or the mood is a good one.

title: One family well used, or two that clearly differ
text: A single family in a few weights can carry a whole film. When a second family is added, make it clearly different in kind, a display face against a plain text face, so the pairing reads as a choice. Two similar typefaces look like a mistake. Match the character of the type to the subject, firm, friendly, technical or elegant, and keep it throughout.
see: Set two lines in the candidate pair. If you cannot tell at once that they are different faces, they are too close.

title: Spacing that follows size
text: Large display type usually wants tighter spacing, small text wants looser, and capitals want a little extra room. Adjusting spacing and line height by size is one of the quiet differences between type that is set and type that is merely placed. Check the awkward pairs of letters in the largest words, where gaps show most.
see: Look at the biggest word. Uneven gaps between its letters will be obvious at that size.

title: Margins that survive every screen
text: Keep the important content away from the edges by a consistent margin, bigger for vertical films where interface overlays cover the top and bottom. Elements that touch the edge by accident look cropped; elements that leave the frame by design should clearly be moving. A steady margin is also what makes a layout look calm.
see: Overlay the format's safe zone mentally. Text inside the margin everywhere is safe.

title: An alignment the eye can find
text: Align things to a few shared lines, a left edge, a centre, a baseline, and the frame feels ordered even when it is full. Items that almost line up are worse than items that clearly do not. Keep the same grid from shot to shot so that elements sit where the eye expects them, and break the grid once for emphasis.
see: Draw a line down the left edges of the text blocks. They should fall on the same few lines.

title: Reveal in the order of reading
text: Bring things in the order the viewer should take them: the headline, then the support, then the detail. Showing everything at once forces the viewer to choose, and they will choose badly. A sequenced reveal also builds a small rhythm inside the shot. Hold the whole picture for a moment once it is complete so it can be read as a whole.
see: Describe the order in which things appear. It should match the order in which you want them read.

title: A transition that says something
text: Use a transition when it carries meaning: a wipe that follows a movement already on screen, a flash that matches a hit, a zoom that goes through an object into the next scene. A hard cut is a fine transition when picture and sound are lined up. The question is always what the change from one shot to the next is meant to feel like.
see: For each cut ask what it communicates. 'Nothing, it is just there' is the answer to remove.

title: Sound in layers
text: Build the sound from a bed that holds the film together, accents that mark the moves, and silences that give them weight. The bed sets the pace, the accents are sparse enough to be felt, and the voice, when there is one, sits above them all with room to be heard. Sound effects on every element become noise; on the key ones they become emphasis.
see: Listen with your eyes closed. You should be able to tell where the important moments are.

title: A voice clear above the music
text: Duck the music while someone speaks, smoothly and by a clear amount, and bring it back in the pauses. The voice should be understood on small speakers at low volume, so check it there. Music with its own melody under a voice competes for the same ear; pick or prepare music that leaves the speech band free.
see: Play the film on a phone speaker. Every word of the voice should be intelligible.

title: An interface rebuilt with fidelity
text: When the film shows a product's screen, rebuild it with the care of the real thing: consistent spacing, believable data, the right states, rounded corners and shadows that agree with each other. Then frame it tight enough that the viewer can read what a person would use. A vague gesture at an interface, grey bars for text, looks like a wireframe and weakens the product.
see: Read the texts inside the interface. If they are lines of grey, the screen is not yet the product.

title: Tilt a plane to give a screen a place
text: A flat screen facing the camera is a diagram. Turn it a few degrees in perspective, let it catch a highlight, give it a shadow beneath, and it becomes an object in a room. Keep the tilt modest where the content must be read, and larger only for a passing glimpse. The move that straightens it into reading position is a natural payoff.
see: Ask whether the screen could be mistaken for a screenshot pasted into the frame.

title: Kinetic type that carries the idea
text: Moving type works when the movement means something: a word that grows as the claim grows, letters that stack as the figures add up, a line that is wiped as the idea is dropped. The motion should follow the voice or the music, and each word should be readable at the moment it matters. Decorative wobble on every letter makes the words harder to read, not livelier.
see: Ask what the movement of each word says. If the answer is 'it looks lively', the movement is decoration.

title: An object given the stage
text: When a physical thing is the subject, give it a stage: a clean background, a clear light from one side, a surface to sit on, room around it, and a slow turn or a push that reveals its form. Show it whole before showing details. One object per idea reads clearly; a pile of objects is a catalogue. Let a reflection or a shadow tie it to the ground.
see: Look for how the object touches the ground or the light. Without a shadow or a reflection it floats.

title: A diagram that draws itself in order
text: Build a diagram the way it would be explained: the first element, then what it connects to, then the next, each arriving as the voice names it. Highlight the part under discussion and quiet the rest. A finished diagram shown whole from the first frame is a map the viewer has to decode; one that grows is a story.
see: Check that each element appears as it is mentioned, not before.

title: A photograph treated as part of the world
text: A photograph placed unchanged next to designed elements usually looks borrowed. Bring it into the film's palette with a grade, a tint or a duotone, crop it deliberately, and give it the same kind of edge, shadow or grain as everything else. A well-chosen photograph at full frame, with the type set on its quiet area, needs no more treatment than a good crop.
see: Compare the photograph's colour temperature with the plate around it. If they disagree, the photograph is not integrated.

title: A character who does something
text: A figure on screen should act: point, react, walk through the scene, hand something over. A character standing in a corner as decoration draws the eye for no reason. Keep the design simple and consistent from shot to shot, and let the motion carry the personality, with anticipation before a move and follow-through after it.
see: Ask what the character is doing for the viewer in this shot. Nothing means it should go.

title: A map that travels
text: On a map, the story is movement: a route drawn between two places, a camera that follows it, labels that appear only for the places in the story. Strip the map of everything else so the path reads. Zoom out far enough to show scale, then close enough to show the destination, and let the transition between the two be one continuous move.
see: Count the labels. Any place not mentioned in the story should have no name on screen.

title: The shape of a launch film
text: A launch film builds in beats: the promise, the product shown up close, two or three proofs, one moment of delight, and the way to get it. Each beat is a few seconds and each has its own look within the same system. The product should be on screen early and often, and the numbers or features should be claimed in the viewer's terms, not the maker's.
see: Mark the beat of each shot. A launch that spends half its length on setup has not yet shown the product.

title: The shape of an explainer
text: An explainer starts from a problem the viewer recognises, introduces one idea at a time in the order they depend on each other, and ends with the thing they can now do. Each idea gets a visual that is the idea, not an illustration beside it. Cut anything that is true but not needed for the next step.
see: After each shot ask whether the viewer could now say the idea in their own words.

title: A teaser that withholds
text: A teaser promises more than it shows: fragments, a sound, a close detail, the edge of something, then a date or a name. Its power is in what it leaves out, so resist the urge to explain. Keep it short, make the cuts quick and rhythmic, and end on the single frame that will make people want the rest.
see: Ask what the viewer cannot yet say about the subject after watching. The answer should be intriguing.

title: An ad with a single message
text: A short ad has room for one message, said three ways: seen, heard and written. Everything else is cut. The brand appears early enough to be remembered and returns at the end with the action. The tone should match the audience: confident for professionals, warm for families, wry for those who dislike being sold to.
see: Write the message in one sentence. Each shot should be an instance of it.

title: A tutorial that follows the hand
text: In a tutorial the viewer's eye follows the cursor or the hand, so the camera should too: zoom to where the action is, show the result, return to the whole. Mark each step briefly and keep the pace slow enough to copy. A recording shown at full width with the action in a tiny corner teaches nobody anything.
see: At every click, is the target big enough to read on a phone?

title: An announcement with weight
text: News gets its authority from restraint: few elements, steady type, unhurried pace, a clear first line and a clear date or consequence. Let the statement sit on screen long enough to be read twice. Excess motion makes an announcement look like an advertisement, and the viewer will trust it less.
see: Remove every effect that is not needed. If the announcement still reads, the effects were noise.

title: Dressing that serves the speaker
text: Dressing a talking video means adding what the speech asks for: a title where a topic starts, an illustration where an image helps, captions in the language and rhythm of the voice, a zoom at an emphasis. Each addition is justified by the words. Added effects with no relation to what is said, however polished, pull attention away from the person.
see: For each addition, find the word in the speech that it answers.

title: A data story with a before and an after
text: Numbers mean something against a comparison: last year, the competitor, the target. Show the starting point first, then let the change happen on screen, and land on the figure that matters with its unit and its meaning in a short line. Label directly on the marks rather than in a separate legend, and cut the axes down to what the eye needs.
see: Ask what the number is compared with. If nothing, it is a decoration.

title: Legible at the format it will be watched in
text: Design for the smallest screen that will show the film. A vertical film is mostly watched in the hand, so the type must be larger than seems necessary on a desktop monitor, and the detail in the picture simpler. Check a frame at the size of a thumbnail and again held at arm's length. What disappears at that size does not belong in the shot.
see: Shrink a frame to thumbnail size. The main idea should still be recognisable.

title: Direction carried across cuts
text: Movement that leaves the frame on one side feels natural entering on the opposite side of the next shot; a push in followed by another push in builds momentum; a push followed by a pull gives the cut a pulse. Choose the direction deliberately at each cut, rather than letting each shot be designed alone, and the film gains a sense of travelling somewhere.
see: Draw an arrow for the main movement of each shot. The sequence of arrows should make a pattern.

title: Land the last frame, or loop it
text: Decide how the film ends its life: a final frame composed to be held and read, or a last frame that matches the first so the film can loop without a seam. Both are intentional; a film that merely runs out at the end of the music is neither. Check the exact last frame, since it is the one used as a thumbnail in many places.
see: Export the final frame as a still. It should be a picture worth keeping.

title: The empty scene
text: A scene made of a plain background and one line of text. It may be tasteful in a still, but in a film it reads as a pause the maker did not fill. The viewer feels the absence of something to look at, and the film's level of finish drops with it.
see: Cover the text. If nothing else on screen is worth looking at, the scene is empty.
fix: Give the scene a subject: the object, the interface, the chart or the picture the words are about, with light and texture around it.

title: One form in every scene
text: Every scene has the same layout: a centred title over a card, or a row of three boxes, repeated with different words. The content changes and the form does not, so the film feels like a template. The viewer stops looking after the second scene because they know what the third will be.
see: Line up the thumbnails of all scenes. If you could swap their texts without anyone noticing, the form repeats.
fix: Change the kind of picture, not the colours: an interface here, a large word there, an object, a chart, a diagram.

title: Generic motion: everything fades and slides up
text: Every element enters with the same fade and small upward slide, at the same speed, in the same order. It is safe and it says nothing. Motion that is identical for a headline, a number and a button cannot tell the viewer which matters.
see: Watch three entrances in a row. If you could not say which belongs to which element, the motion is generic.
fix: Give the entrance a reason: scale and weight for the hero, a quick tick for the small items, a movement that follows the direction of the story.

title: Material that does not match
text: A photograph beside flat vector shapes, a glossy render beside a paper cut-out, a hand-drawn figure on a clean interface. Each is fine alone, and together they look assembled from different sources. The viewer senses that the pieces do not belong to one world.
see: Name the material of each object in the frame. If the names clash, so does the frame.
fix: Choose one material language and bring the outliers into it with the same grade, edge, shadow and grain.

title: A palette that drifts
text: The accent is blue in the first scenes, teal in the middle and purple at the end, or the neutrals shift from warm to cool without a reason. No single choice looks wrong, but the film loses its identity and the accent stops meaning anything.
see: Sample the accent in the first and the last scene. If they differ, the palette drifted.
fix: Define the palette once as tokens and reference them everywhere; change a token, never a value in one layer.

title: Text too small for the format
text: Type that is comfortable on a desktop preview becomes a smudge on a phone. Small captions, legal lines, labels inside interfaces and figures on axes are the usual victims. The viewer cannot read them and may not notice they are there, so they add clutter and no information.
see: View the film at the size it will be watched. Whatever you cannot read at once is too small.
fix: Enlarge it, or remove it. If it matters, make it a headline; if it does not, delete it.

title: The logo too early
text: The brand mark fills the first seconds before the viewer has any reason to care. It spends the strongest attention of the film on the least interesting information, and it makes the film feel like an advertisement from the first frame.
see: Look at the first three seconds. If the only content is a name and a mark, the logo is early.
fix: Open with the promise or the picture, and bring the logo in at the end, with the action.

title: A transition on every cut
text: Each change of scene has a wipe, a flash or a zoom. The effect that was meant to link shots becomes the most visible thing about them, and because it happens every time, it stops being an event. The film feels slower, since every cut needs time to play out.
see: Count the cuts and count the transitions. If the numbers match, they are not doing a job.
fix: Keep a transition only where it carries a meaning, and let the others be hard cuts lined up with the music.

title: Sound on every element
text: Every text, shape and movement has its own whoosh, pop or tick. The soundtrack becomes a continuous clatter in which no single sound stands out, and the music is buried under it. A film where everything makes a noise has no loud moment left.
see: Listen to the effects alone. If they sound like a constant rain, there are too many.
fix: Keep effects for the few key moves and the hero, and let the rest of the film breathe on the music.

title: A frame without light
text: Shapes of flat colour on a flat colour, with no gradient, glow, shadow or texture to say where anything is. The frame looks like a slide, however well it is composed, because nothing in it has volume or a source of light.
see: Look for a highlight and a shadow. If there are none, the frame has no light.
fix: Add a source: a soft glow behind the subject, a gradient across the ground, a shadow under the object, a touch of grain.

title: Type in three families
text: A display face for titles, a different one for captions and a third in the interfaces, none of them chosen to go together. The film looks like it was assembled from other people's work, and the voice of the type, which should be steady, changes from shot to shot.
see: List the typefaces used. More than two is too many.
fix: Pick one family, or one display face with one text face, and use only those.

title: A placeholder left in
text: Lorem ipsum, a square where a picture should be, 'Your name here', a figure that is plainly invented round numbers. One such thing in a corner is enough to undo the credibility of the rest. The viewer does not need to read it to feel that the film is unfinished.
see: Search every text and every picture slot for words like placeholder, lorem or a grey box.
fix: Replace each with the real thing from the brief, or remove the element.

title: The speaker alone for thirty seconds
text: A talking video where nothing changes on screen but the person's face for half a minute. Even a good speaker loses the viewer at that length, because the picture has stopped adding to the words. The retention drops where the picture stops moving.
see: Find the longest stretch with only the speaker. Over twenty seconds is a gap.
fix: Cover it: an illustration of what is said, a key word, a change of framing, a title over the speaker.

title: Repeated compositions
text: Two or three shots in a row use the same arrangement, the subject in the same place at the same scale, with only the content changed. The eye reads the repetition as a lack of ideas rather than as a rhythm, and the cuts between them carry no energy.
see: Overlay the thumbnails of consecutive shots. If the shapes coincide, the composition repeats.
fix: Change the scale, the side or the angle of the subject at each cut, so that consecutive shots differ clearly.

title: A camera drift with no reason
text: A slow, constant zoom or pan applied to every shot to keep it alive. It is meant to add movement and instead adds a feeling of unease, because the motion has no destination. The viewer senses that the camera is going somewhere and then finds it was going nowhere.
see: Ask where each camera move ends and why. A move that ends on nothing in particular is a drift.
fix: Cut the drift, or turn it into a move with a target: push in on the detail that matters, then hold.

title: Everything is the hero
text: Every scene has its biggest move, loudest hit and boldest framing. With no quiet to contrast against, none of them lands, and the film is tiring after the first half minute. The climax disappears because the whole film is at its level.
see: Rate each scene's intensity from one to ten. A row of eights and nines has no peak.
fix: Choose one hero, lower the rest, and give the hero a silence before it.

title: Text over a busy ground
text: Words set directly on a photograph, a video or a detailed pattern, with no plate, shadow or calm area behind them. In the best frame the text can be read; in the worst it vanishes. The viewer cannot predict which, so they stop trying.
see: Scrub through the shot looking for the worst frame under the text. If you cannot read it there, the text fails.
fix: Place the text on a quiet area, or add a plate, a gradient shade or a blur behind it.

title: Several things of the same weight
text: A headline, a subhead, three stat blocks and a button, all about the same size and weight. The eye has no entry point and wanders, and the viewer reads whichever caught their eye first, which is rarely the one you meant.
see: Squint. If nothing stands out, nothing is first.
fix: Choose the first, second and third things, and scale them so the order is plain. Remove what is not in the first three.

title: Motion at a constant speed
text: Elements slide, scale and rotate at an even pace from start to finish, as though on rails. It looks mechanical and cheap, because nothing in the physical world starts and stops instantly. The effect is most visible on large elements and on camera moves.
see: Check the spacing of positions across a move. Equal gaps mean a linear move.
fix: Apply an ease with a soft start and a long settle, and give larger things slower eases.

title: Everything enters at once
text: All the elements of a scene appear on the same frame, so the viewer is handed the whole picture with no guidance. It is hard to read and it wastes the opportunity of the entrance, which is the best moment to direct attention.
see: Step to the frame where the scene appears. If all its elements are there already, nothing was staged.
fix: Stagger the entrances in the order of reading, a few frames apart, with the most important first.

title: Cuts that ignore the music
text: Scene changes fall at arbitrary moments against the beat or the phrase, so picture and sound pull against each other. Occasionally this is a deliberate tension; more often it is the sign that the edit and the music were made separately.
see: Tap the beat while watching. Cuts that are consistently just before or after it are mistimed.
fix: Move each cut onto a downbeat or a phrase end, and choose which logic the passage follows.

title: A film that just stops
text: The last scene is as long as any other, shows nothing the viewer can act on and cuts to black when the music runs out. The film has no final beat, so it leaves no impression and no next step.
see: Freeze the last second. If it has no words, no mark and no held picture, there is no ending.
fix: Compose a final frame with the one line or mark to remember, hold it long enough to read twice, then end.
